findings.title: Provider selection is nondeterministic when highest order is tied
findings.body: detectProvider now sorts all discovered providers by order and returns the first, only logging the rest at debug. All existing built-in providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) still return order 200, so when more than one is visible there is no unique winner and selection depends on ServiceLoader/JAR order. In a FIPS deployment this can silently select the non-FIPS provider, or at minimum construct/register both providers' global security state before ignoring one, defeating FIPS compliance. The previous code failed fast on multiple providers. The selection should fail on a tie for the highest order or the built-in providers need distinct orders.

findings.title: Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: order() was added to the public CryptoProvider SPI as an abstract method. Third-party implementations compiled against the previous version do not implement it, so ServiceLoader can instantiate them but CryptoIntegration.detectProvider's call to CryptoProvider::order throws AbstractMethodError, breaking all crypto initialization. Make order() a default method with a defined fallback order, or otherwise preserve compatibility with legacy providers.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JVM default KeyStore provider
findings.body: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the JVM default KeyStore type, which is normally SUN, not BouncyCastle. The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning the BouncyCastle security provider, and callers may use the returned provider to resolve BC-specific algorithms or to obtain a provider name. Returning SUN silently gives such callers the wrong provider. Since this minimal authz-client provider has no BouncyCastle dependency, it should return null or throw UnsupportedOperationException rather than return an unrelated provider.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests do not use P-384/P-521 keys
findings.body: The test class creates one default EC key pair (typically P-256) and reuses it for testES256, testES384 and testES512. The ES384 and ES512 cases therefore only exercise padding a P-256 signature to 96/132 bytes; they never exercise real P-384/P-521-sized r and s values, nor verify the produced ASN.1 DER against the key. A regression that mishandles full-size ES384/ES512 signatures could pass. Generate the matching curve key pair per algorithm, or use fixed vectors and verify the result.
